title: std::move That Doesn't Move
explanation:
`std::move` doesn't move anything. It's only a cast to an rvalue reference (`T&&`), which *allows* overload resolution to pick a move constructor.

`std::move(a)` has type `std::string&&`, so `b` is move-constructed and steals `a`'s buffer. (`a` is left "valid but unspecified"; that's why the program doesn't print it.)

`std::move(c)` has type `const std::string&&`. The move constructor takes a non-const `std::string&&` because it must modify its source, so it can't bind. The copy constructor (`const std::string&`) can, so `d` is a **copy** and `c` still holds `world`.

Lesson: `std::move` on a `const` object silently copies. This also happens when you `return std::move(member)` from a `const` member function.
